sources.news_title: US Federal Judge Dismisses Trump Administration Seeking Harvard Admissions Records
sources.text:
Diyar Guldogan
03 November 2026•Update: 03 November 2026
A federal judge on Monday dismissed a lawsuit by the Trump administration seeking to compel Harvard University to hand over detailed admissions records as part of a federal investigation into alleged racial discrimination.
US District Judge Myong J. Joun of the District of Massachusetts dismissed the case without prejudice, finding that the federal government had failed to adequately demonstrate that it followed the required administrative procedures before seeking judicial enforcement.
In his ruling, Joun found that the Department of Justice (DOJ) had not sufficiently established that it notified Harvard of the specific compliance failures and the enforcement action it intended to pursue before filing the lawsuit.
The Department of Education also failed to demonstrate that it had completed the required steps to secure voluntary compliance before referring the matter for judicial enforcement.
The lawsuit sought detailed applicant-level admissions information from Harvard, including academic records, race and ethnicity data, essays and admissions decisions. The requests were part of federal reviews examining whether the university complied with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
The judge emphasized that federal agencies must follow established statutory and regulatory procedures before asking courts to enforce administrative information demands.
The dismissal, however, does not prevent the Trump administration from filing another lawsuit after addressing the procedural deficiencies identified by the court.
Joun also made clear that his decision does not resolve whether Harvard must ultimately provide the requested admissions records or whether the government's demands are legally justified.
The ruling represents a procedural setback for the administration's efforts to obtain Harvard's admissions data while leaving the underlying federal investigation into the university's admissions practices unresolved.

sources.news_title: Federal judge dismisses Trump administration's Harvard admissions case
sources.text:
Nov. 2 (UPI) — A federal judge on Monday dismissed a lawsuit by the Trump administration seeking to force Harvard University to turn over records for a federal investigation into its admissions decisions.
The U.S. Justice Department filed the lawsuit in February, saying that Harvard allegedly failed to comply with its investigation, which sought to confirm the university followed a Supreme Court ruling banning affirmative action in college admissions.
It later added an investigation from the U.S. Education Department. Both departments have started numerous investigations into whether colleges continue to consider race in admissions.
The Justice Department sought admissions documents including application essays written by individual students. It said Harvard “slow-walked” the process to hand over the documents and refused to hand over other materials related to its decisions.
On Monday, Judge Myong J. Joun of the Massachusetts District Court ruled neither department could prove it followed the required procedural steps before suing Harvard.
“A deadline and a threat to sue, standing alone, do not necessarily demonstrate compliance” with the Justice Department’s process for working with schools over information demands, Joun wrote.
Harvard was part of the 2023 Supreme Court case Students for Fair Admissions vs. Harvard that led to the scrapping of affirmative action in college admissions.
In the case dismissed Monday, the university argued that the government information demands were overly broad and could reveal identifying and sensitive information about thousands of applicants. It said it had already turned over many documents on admission procedures and that the lawsuit was part of “the Trump administration’s ongoing campaign against Harvard.”
Joun did not rule on whether Harvard has discriminated against applicants or other questions around the case, including if the university may still be required to provide the documents.
The case was dismissed without prejudice, meaning that it can be refiled. A spokesperson for the Justice Department said that it will do so.

Judge dismisses lawsuit against Harvard over federal demand for admissions data
sources.text:
Judge dismisses lawsuit against Harvard over federal demand for admissions data
A federal judge has dismissed a lawsuit against Harvard University over its alleged failure to provide admissions records that the Justice Department demanded to ensure the Ivy League school stopped using affirmative action in admissions
BOSTON -- A federal judge on Monday dismissed a lawsuit against Harvard University over its alleged failure to provide admissions records that the Justice Department had demanded to ensure the Ivy League school stopped using affirmative action in admissions.
The Justice Department said Harvard had “thwarted” efforts to investigate potential discrimination. It accused Harvard of refusing to comply with a federal investigation and asked a judge to order the university to turn over the records.
But U.S. District Judge Myong Joun concluded that the Justice Department didn't take the necessary procedural steps to obtain the data before filing the lawsuit. “Before taking enforcement action under the statutory framework, the agency must advise the recipient of its failure to comply and determine that compliance cannot be secured by voluntary means,” Joun wrote.
But Joun also said the ruling does not end the dispute over the data.
“I decide a limited question: whether the Government has adequately established, at this stage and on the materials properly considered, that it satisfied the prerequisites to judicial enforcement invoked in this complaint,” he wrote. “The ruling does not determine whether Harvard has discriminated, whether the agencies may lawfully seek appropriately defined applicant-level data, or whether Harvard may ultimately be required to provide such data.”
Neither Harvard nor the Department of Justice responded to a request for comment.
The ruling is the latest setback against the Trump administration over its ongoing battle with Harvard. It has suffered defeats in the federal courts over everything from billions of dollars in funding cuts to a lawsuit accusing the university of antisemitism.
Trump officials have said they’re taking action against Harvard over allegations of anti-Jewish bias on campus. Harvard officials say they’re facing unconstitutional retaliation for refusing to adopt the administration’s ideological views.
In the fight over admissions data, the Justice Department in 2025 launched a compliance review into Harvard’s admissions practices. It told Harvard to hand over five years of admissions data for applicants to its undergraduate, medial and law schools.
It also asked Harvard for applicants’ grades, test scores, essays, extracurricular activities and admissions outcomes, along with their race and ethnicity.
Justice Department officials said they need the data to determine whether Harvard has continued considering applicants’ race in admissions decisions. The Supreme Court barred affirmative action in admissions in 2023 after lawsuits challenged it at Harvard and the University of North Carolina.
The effort against Harvard is part of a broader campaign by the Trump administration against colleges accused of considering race in admissions decisions.
In October, the Justice Department found the law school at the University of California, Los Angeles, illegally considered race in admissions. The announcement follows a similar finding against the university’s medical school.
The administration also has accused the UC Berkeley Law School and the medical school at the University of California, San Diego, of illegally discriminating against white and Asian applicants.

sources.news_title: Federal Judge Dismisses Admissions Lawsuit Against Harvard
sources.text:
Federal Judge Dismisses Admissions Lawsuit Against Harvard
A district court judge dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit seeking individual applicant records from Harvard on Monday afternoon, finding that the government failed to meet procedural requirements before suing the University.
Judge Myoung J. Joun’s 10-page opinion did not rule on the merits of the records request, leaving open the possibility that the government could bring a new lawsuit if it corrected its procedural missteps.
The dismissal marks a win for Harvard in a prolonged dispute over whether the University must hand over applicant-level admissions data to prove it is complying with the Supreme Court’s 2023 decision barring race-conscious admissions.
The Justice Department sued Harvard in February to compel the University to hand over the records, arguing that it had “thwarted” and “slow-walked” a federal civil rights review by failing to meet deadlines for multiple records requests.
Harvard asked Joun to throw out the case on procedural grounds in June. He granted that request on Monday, finding that the Justice Department failed to demonstrate that it took the necessary steps to seek voluntary compliance before it moved to judicial enforcement.
Joun cited two procedural shortcomings in the government’s complaint: It did not allege the Justice Department had informed Harvard that it would sue if the University did not comply, or that it had communicated the “specific failure identified” to Harvard.
“A deadline and a threat to sue, standing alone, do not necessarily demonstrate compliance with the regulatory voluntary-compliance process where the agency seeks to enforce disputed demands for extensive information,” Joun wrote.
Joun also found that the Education Department failed to follow the proper procedural steps before folding its own admissions probe into the DOJ lawsuit in May.
Get The Crimson in your inbox.
Harvard, the Department of Education, and the Department of Justice did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
At a September oral argument, Joun expressed skepticism about the government’s efforts to negotiate with Harvard before suing, describing its stance at one point as an “ultimatum.”
Harvard, for its part, has maintained that it provided the government with as much information as possible — more than 2,000 pages of documents — without divulging individualized records, which it says are privileged.
Harvard’s lawyers have also argued that the DOJ prematurely abandoned negotiations with the University in favor of litigation to advance a retaliatory campaign against Harvard for rebuffing the Trump administration’s demands last year.
Legal experts have separately said that the government’s information request could run up against the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, a landmark statute restricting access to educational records.
The dismissal comes less than a week after Harvard College released demographic data for its Class of 2030 showing the proportion of enrolled Black students fell for the third consecutive year since the Supreme Court’s affirmative action ruling. The share of Black students in the Class of 2030 dropped to 9.3 percent, while the proportion of Asian American students rose to 43.2 percent.
Joun’s ruling did not address either the validity of the government’s records request or whether the lawsuit was brought “for an improper or retaliatory purpose.”
“Those questions remain open,” Joun wrote. “Nothing in this decision converts the Government’s request for information into an accusation of present discrimination or resolves Harvard’s underlying Title VI compliance.”

sources.news_title: US judge dismisses Trump administration’s Harvard admissions probe case - Regional Media News
sources.text:
By Nate Raymond
BOSTON, Nov 2 (Reuters) – A federal judge on Monday dismissed a lawsuit by President Donald Trump’s administration seeking to force Harvard University to turn over records for an investigation into whether it continues to consider race in its student admissions process.
US District Judge Myong Joun in Boston rejected the US Department of Justice’s lawsuit, which Harvard contends was filed as part of a broader campaign by the Republican president’s administration against the Ivy League school.
The judge stressed that his decision rested on narrow, procedural grounds and did not resolve whether the Justice Department and US Department of Education could ultimately seek data on thousands of high school students who sought admission at Harvard.
But Joun, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, agreed with Harvard that the Justice Department sued without taking all legally required steps aimed at securing the university’s voluntary compliance with its demands for applicant-level data.
“For example, the complaint does not allege that DOJ informed Harvard of the action it would take – namely, litigation – should Harvard fail to comply, nor does the complaint allege the specific failure identified,” Joun wrote.
The Justice Department and Harvard did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Harvard has been a top target of the administration’s effort to leverage federal funding and government power to force changes at universities that Trump says are dominated by “radical left” ideologies.
The Cambridge, Massachusetts-based university has already secured rulings from other judges rejecting the administration’s efforts to terminate over $2 billion in grants, block the school from hosting international students and sue it for allegedly failing to protect Jewish and Israeli students from harassment.
The Justice Department filed the case before Joun in February, arguing that Harvard was not complying with investigations into whether it is following the US Supreme Court’s 2023 ruling rejecting race-conscious admissions programs used to boost enrollment of minority students.
The administration said it needed years of applicant-level admissions data to determine whether race remains a factor in Harvard’s admissions decisions and if the university is complying with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which bars racial discrimination in education programs.
The university’s lawyers countered that the case was filed to retaliate against Harvard for refusing demands that it overhaul its governance, hiring and academic programs to align with the administration’s agenda.
They said the lawsuit was filed after Trump announced in early February that he was ending settlement talks and wanted $1 billion in damages from Harvard, which he said had “been, for a long time, behaving very badly.”
Joun, in dismissing the case on Monday, stressed that he was not resolving whether Harvard has discriminated or if it may ultimately be required to provide data to the agencies. The Justice Department could try to pursue a similar case again if it takes additional administrative steps, he said.
(Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani)

sources.news_title: Judge Throws Out Trump Administration’s Affirmative Action Lawsuit Against Harvard
sources.text:
A federal judge has thrown out the Justice Department’s case accusing Harvard University of withholding admissions data from government investigators probing whether the school was complying with the Supreme Court’s 2023 ban on affirmative action.
Massachusetts U.S. District Judge Myong J. Joun dismissed the case but left open an avenue for the government to reopen its complaint against the storied educational institution once it addresses certain procedural issues.
“For these reasons, Harvard’s motion to dismiss is granted without prejudice,” Joun wrote.
Joun said that he did not make a determination on the case’s merits on admission information.
Trending
The lawsuit, filed in February, sought data from hundreds of thousands of college applications — including students’ personal essays — to investigate Harvard’s compliance with new rules rejecting race-conscious admissions. In 2023, the Supreme Court found that affirmative action violates Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin in programs that rely on federal money.
The Justice Department had argued it gave Harvard repeated opportunities to turn over the records.
“Harvard has failed to disclose the data we need to ensure that its admissions are free of discrimination,” then-Attorney General Pamela Bondi said in February. “We will continue fighting to put merit over DEI across America.”
Harvard said that it had provided substantial records for government investigators but objected to the probe’s scope and relevance.
Joun found that the government failed to prove it had tried to settle the issue with the school before taking legal action.
“The Government may be able to identify a qualifying determination or cure the procedural deficiency, but it has not supplied a sufficient basis for the judicial relief currently sought,” Joun wrote.
The ruling still doesn’t answer questions about whether Harvard’s admissions process can be considered discriminatory, or whether the government’s investigation was politically retaliatory.

sources.news_title: Federal judge dismisses administration’s Harvard admissions case
Harvard Wins Against Trump’s Extreme Lawsuit Over Admissions Data
sources.text:
Harvard Wins Against Trump’s Extreme Lawsuit Over Admissions Data
A federal judge has thrown out the Justice Department’s lawsuit against Harvard University.
Michael Fein/Bloomberg/Getty Images
President Trump’s attempt to shake down Harvard University for its admissions data was thrown out by a federal judge Monday.
U.S. District Judge Myong J. Joun in Boston dismissed the White House’s lawsuit against the university, saying that the Department of Justice did not follow all legally required steps to get a court order compelling the university to comply with its demands.
“The ruling does not determine whether Harvard has discriminated, whether the agencies may lawfully seek appropriately defined applicant-level data, or whether Harvard may ultimately be required to provide such data,” Joun wrote in his ruling.
In its lawsuit, the Trump administration claimed that Harvard wasn’t cooperating with a government review of its admissions policies, and “slow-walked the pace of production” of relevant documents and refused to hand over others. Those documents included application essays.
Harvard said the DOJ’s demands were excessive, calling the administration’s lawsuit “part of the Trump administration’s ongoing campaign against Harvard.” The institution said its admissions process was in full accordance with federal law.
Trump demanded $1 billion from the university earlier this year after it refused to sign his “compact” on education policy and send millions of dollars to the U.S. Treasury. The administration also sued Harvard for allegedly fostering a “hostile educational environment” for Jewish and Israeli students, but that lawsuit was thrown out in August.
Trump and his far-right allies have sought to fight “far-left” influence at U.S. universities, using cuts to federal education funding and accusations of antisemitism to force these institutions to comply with right-wing policies and ideology. Harvard is the highest-profile university to be targeted and seems to be successfully fighting back.
JD Vance Kicks Off New Conspiracy to Sow Doubt About Election
The vice president is already trying to blame immigrants for potential Republican losses in a key state.
Tom Brenner/Getty Images
Vice President JD Vance is once again spreading racist lies for attention.
At a midterm elections rally for Republican gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy in Swanton, Ohio, on Monday, Vance baselessly claimed that undocumented immigrants were engaged in a plot to steal the state’s election.
“Now, I saw a story, just in the last couple of days, that there are illegal communities of illegal immigrant Somalis who are coordinating to flood the polls and drown out your vote,” Vance said. “Well, I happen to believe that we want American elections to belong to American citizens. Send a message by voting for Vivek for governor!”
Vance: I saw a story that there are illegal communities of illegal immigrant Somalis who are coordinating to flood the polls and drown out your vote. We want American elections to belong to American citizens. Send a message by voting for Vivek for governor. https://t.co/PsTT7ScDQI
There is no evidence to support Vance’s claim, and it’s unclear what “story” he is supposedly referring to.
If you’re feeling a sense of déjà vu, that’s because this isn’t the first time the vice president has indulged in this kind of grotesque gossip. While campaigning with President Donald Trump ahead of the 2024 presidential election, Vance spread false rumors that Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, were eating their neighbors’ cats and dogs. Later, he admitted that he had absolutely no evidence to support his claims. “If I have to create stories so that the American media actually pays attention to the suffering of the American people then that’s what I’m going to do,” he said at the time.
With just hours until Election Day, it seems that Vance may be back to his old tricks, turning his attention to another immigrant community that Trump has attacked with racist smears. And unlike the Somali community in Minnesota, which has broad support from the state’s Democratic-led government, right-wing lawmakers have repeatedlytargeted Ohio’s Somali American community.
Trump Hosts Bizarre Show-and-Tell With Photos of Reflecting Pool
On the eve of the midterm elections, Donald Trump talked all about his meaningless renovations in Washington, D.C.
Donald Trump points to a photo of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool while standing in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
Donald Trump points to a photo of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool while standing in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
Instead of making a sober and succinct pitch to voters on the final day before a consequential midterm election, President Trump decided to spend most of his speech rambling about Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovations.
“Today I’m thrilled to announce the official opening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool,” he said Monday afternoon, before making a joke that he planned on changing the name to the “Trump Reflecting Pool.”
“The pool is now better and more beautiful than it’s ever been before. And we went through a lot with vandalism. The vandalism was unprecedented,” Trump continued, again pushing the spurious claim that leftist criminals—not his own poor design decisions—were responsible for the “American flag blue” paint at the bottom of the pool peeling off.
Trump on the Reflecting Pool: "We went through a lot with vandalism. The vandalism was unprecedented. People don't like talking about it." https://t.co/9mhZNdPpTZ
Trump then turned to the show-and-tell portion of his speech, pulling out a series of pictures of algae, graffiti, and other issues with the renovations and analyzing them live, as if he had just seen the photos for the first time.
“These are the pipes.… You know it’s been there since 1922, I guess. It’s in bad shape.… [There were] tremendous algae problems. You have that picture with the algae?” he asked an aide. “Yeah, lemme see that. This was a picture taken just before they closed it down. And this picture, this was in the Biden era.… They just spend money after money after money. It’s not an easy thing. The algae’s brutal, it forms easily, and we have it.… That’s not grass, that’s algae.”
"You have that picture with the algae?" -- President Trump's closing midterms message https://t.co/x3tMssccca
“I can’t believe he is actually making his closing argument speech about the reflecting pool renovations,” liberal podcaster and former Obama staffer Tommy Vietor wrote. “This is a bad resistance lib joke come to life.”
While the president eventually did get to more pressing issues, the first 15 minutes of his speech were spent talking about something the vast majority of Americans have no reason to care about at all. People across the country are reeling from Trump’s litany of broken promises, with this new forever war on Iran and the spiking cost of living. That’s nothing to say of other failures, like the DOJ’s botched release of the Epstein files. There’s more than one reason his approval rating is incredibly low, and it sure looks like it’s about to haunt Republicans on Tuesday.
Representative Haley Stevens speaks with Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers in the background, on November 1.
Democratic Representative Haley Stevens’s endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers for the Senate in Michigan came out of nowhere, and a train-wreck interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper hours later didn’t answer anyone’s questions as to why she pulled her support from Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
Instead, she decided to offer a full explanation to Olivia Reingold of right-wing outlet The Free Press, who interviewed Stevens at her fiancé Justin Turkish’s home at 11 p.m. Sunday night in the Detroit suburbs. Stevens said she decided to endorse Rogers because she “wasn’t being honest with myself after a certain point.”
The congresswoman told Reingold that it came down to El-Sayed being “obsessive” regarding Israel, pointing to his refusal to say whether Israel or Iran was a greater threat to America in a debate with Rogers. She said his statement in late September that “it is the responsibility of the people of Iran to decide what their leadership should look like” was a refusal to condemn the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps. She said that Iran is the “opposite of our friend.”
The final straw for Stevens, she told Reingold, was a Rebellion PAC TV ad supporting El-Sayed that attributed the rising price of groceries to U.S. support of Israel killing Palestinians. While El-Sayed’s campaign was not involved in the ad and has disavowed it, Stevens thinks that he is holding “anti-American” positions.
In response to Stevens’s endorsement, El-Sayed accused Stevens of “relitigating a primary that ended three months ago” and urged Democrats to rally together to defeat Rogers. Stevens claimed his statement went against the wishes of Jewish voters.
“God, I wanted to vote for him, but he just kind of said ‘Forget it,’” Stevens said. “I love the Democrats. I’m not trying to take anything from anyone or judge anybody or shame anybody.”
Stevens is in no position to accuse someone else of being obsessed with Israel. Her own Senate campaign was heavily funded by AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups, and she has a long and loud history of vocally supporting Israel. During the Democratic primary, El-Sayed’s campaign highlighted a clip from 2023 in which Stevens shouted, “Israel comes to me in my dreams” at a Hanukkah celebration.
That Stevens betrayed the Democratic Party, spurning leading party figures who reached out to her for days hoping to keep her in the fold, and then decided to complain about it all to a right-wing outlet founded by Bari Weiss says all you need to know.
Donald Trump mulled shielding Musk and some of his other allies.
Win McNamee/Getty Images
President Donald Trump suggested Monday that he was open to pardoning Elon Musk.
During a pretaped interview on the New York Post’s Pod Force One, host Miranda Devine asked Trump about concerns that Democrats were plotting to arrest Musk, seize his factories, and nationalize SpaceX. (Of course, no Democratic lawmaker or candidate has actually called for any of that.)
“It won’t happen. It’s talk. But if it is talk, we’ll have to protect them,” Trump said.
Devine asked whether Trump would consider preemptively pardoning Musk and other allies who’d worked for his administration.
“Well, that’s what [Joe] Biden did. He gave everybody a pardon,” Trump said, referring to members of a committee who investigated the deadly January 6 riot.
“I would if I needed to, sure. I would not even think about it. I’d do it, I did it for J6,” he added.
If Democrats win back one or both chambers of Congress, they have signaled they plan to investigate Musk’s shady leadership of the defunct Department of Government Efficiency, his companies’ lucrative contracts with the federal government, and his alleged role in cutting Ukraine’s Starlink access, perhaps on behalf of his close friend Russian President Vladimir Putin.
